headline: March CPI Accelerates to +2.4% as Record Gasoline Surge Reverses Six Months of Disinflation; BoC Faces April 29 Decision with Bond Markets Pricing Year-End Tightening
executive_summary:
Statistics Canada reported March headline CPI at +2.4% year-over-year, up 0.6 percentage points from February's +1.8%, the sharpest monthly acceleration since mid-2022.1 Gasoline prices surged +21.2% month-over-month — the largest monthly increase on record — driven by the Strait of Hormuz disruption that reduced global tanker traffic to near-zero during the blockade.12 CPI excluding gasoline registered +2.2% year-over-year, down from +2.4% ex-gasoline in February, indicating that underlying price pressures moderated even as the energy component spiked.1 Food purchased from stores rose +4.4% year-over-year, with fresh vegetables at +7.8%.1 The project database tracks 6,615 projects valued at $1,161.7B across all sectors, with 4,471 active projects (Proposed, Under Review, and Approved) exposed to shifting financing cost assumptions as bond markets price approximately 41 basis points of tightening by year-end.3

The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive decision on March 18.4 The April 29 rate announcement, accompanied by the Monetary Policy Report, follows the federal Spring Economic Update on April 28.56 Bond markets price an approximately 92% probability of a hold at the April 29 decision, but 2-year Government of Canada yields rose 35 basis points over the period, reflecting a bear-flattening dynamic as traders shifted from pricing cuts to pricing potential hikes.47

The Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March, a partial recovery after February's -84,000 loss, with unemployment unchanged at 6.7%.8 Average hourly wages accelerated to +4.7% year-over-year ($37.73/hr), the fastest pace since October 2024.8 Health care posted the largest year-over-year employment gain at +94,000 (+3.3%), while natural resources added +10,000 (+3.0%) in the month.8 The pipeline tracks 233 healthcare projects ($20.2B) and 344 combined mining and oil and gas projects ($243.3B) in these sectors.

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February, the largest since August 2025, as imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.9 Exports to non-U.S. economies rose +17% year-over-year while exports to the U.S. fell -10% year-over-year, reflecting active trade diversion.910 Manufacturing sales rebounded +3.6% to $71.2B, with unfilled orders at a record $117.6B.11 Housing starts fell 6.0% to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus and well under CMHC's 430,000-480,000/yr affordability target.12 The Bloomberg-Nanos Consumer Confidence Index fell to 46.93, an 11-month low, with only 15% of respondents seeing a stronger economy in six months, down from 27% four weeks prior.13

national.analysis:
Statistics Canada's March Consumer Price Index release recorded headline inflation at +2.4% year-over-year, up from +1.8% in February.1 The 0.6 percentage-point monthly acceleration was driven almost entirely by gasoline, which surged +21.2% month-over-month — the largest single-month gasoline price increase in the history of the series.12 CPI excluding gasoline ran at +2.2% year-over-year, down from +2.4% ex-gasoline in February, suggesting core price dynamics continued to decelerate even as headline inflation spiked.1 Food purchased from stores rose +4.4% year-over-year with fresh vegetables at +7.8%.1 The month-over-month CPI change was +0.9% (seasonally adjusted +0.5%).1 Shelter CPI registered +1.5% year-over-year.14

The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% for its seventh consecutive decision on March 18, with the Summary of Deliberations noting near-term growth weaker than the January Monetary Policy Report projection.4 The April 29 decision will be accompanied by the updated Monetary Policy Report. Bond markets priced an approximately 92% probability of a hold, but the yield curve shifted materially: 2-year Government of Canada yields rose 35 basis points, and markets priced approximately 41 basis points of tightening by year-end — a reversal from rate-cut expectations earlier in 2026.47 The 5-year benchmark yield stood at 3.06% and the 10-year at approximately 3.48%, with the bear-flattening pattern reflecting expectations that the BoC may need to respond to persistent inflation pressures.7 The pipeline tracks 4,471 active projects (Proposed, Under Review, Approved) where financing costs are sensitive to rate-path changes.

The Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March after February's -84,000 loss.8 Unemployment held at 6.7%, with the participation rate at 64.9% and the employment rate at 60.6%.8 Average hourly wages accelerated +0.8 percentage points to +4.7% year-over-year ($37.73/hr), the fastest since October 2024; composition-adjusted wage growth ran at +3.6%.8 Workers aged 55 and older recorded +5.2% wage growth while those aged 15-24 recorded +1.8%.8 By industry, other services added +15,000, professional services +12,000, and natural resources +10,000 (+3.0%), while finance, insurance, and real estate shed -11,000 and accommodation and food services lost -10,000.8 Construction and manufacturing sectors reported the highest hiring difficulty rates at 49.5% and 47.4% respectively.15

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February from a revised $4.2B in January, the largest since August 2025.9 Exports rose 6.4% to $66.3B — the highest since March 2025 — while imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.9 Motor vehicles and parts exports rose +24.2% and precious metals +14.2%.9 Exports to non-U.S. economies rose +17% year-over-year while U.S.-destined exports fell -10% year-over-year, consistent with ongoing trade diversion amid the U.S.-Canada tariff environment.910 Canada announced a six-month pause on retaliatory tariffs for U.S.-origin manufacturing, food/beverage, health care, and national security goods on April 15; the CUSMA joint review is scheduled for July 2026.1625 The pipeline tracks 69 transport and logistics projects ($27.3B) and 45 manufacturing projects ($67.3B) with exposure to shifting trade corridors.

Manufacturing sales rebounded +3.6% to $71.2B in February, led by transport equipment (+18.8%) and primary metals (+4.9% to a record $6.5B).11 Unfilled manufacturing orders reached a record $117.6B.11 Building permits fell 8.4% to $12.1B in February, with non-residential permits declining $1.3B while residential permits added $135.6M.17

CMHC housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus.12 The six-month trend decreased 2.9% to 248,378.12 Year-to-date actual starts ran +9% year-over-year at 49,206 units through March.12 Against CMHC's affordability target of 430,000-480,000 starts per year, the current pace leaves a structural gap.12 The pipeline tracks 166 residential projects ($31.9B) and 1,032 infrastructure projects ($135.4B) that include transit and water/wastewater infrastructure enabling housing development. Real GDP contracted 0.2% quarter-over-quarter (-0.6% annualized) in Q4 2025, down from +0.6% in Q3; Q1 2026 is tracking at +0.8% SAAR according to National Bank of Canada, with full-year forecasts ranging from 1.1% to 1.8%.18

consumer_pulse:
The Bloomberg-Nanos Canadian Consumer Confidence Index fell to 46.93 for the week ended April 3, an 11-month low, as the Iran conflict entered its sixth week and gasoline prices spiked at the pump.1329 The expectations sub-index lost approximately 10 points over four weeks. Only 15% of respondents saw a stronger economy in six months, down from 27% four weeks prior; only 13% reported personal finances had improved over the past year, down from 15%; and approximately 59% reported feeling somewhat secure in their jobs, a slight decrease from the prior period.13

Consumer spending data for Q1 2026 showed total spending at -0.27% year-over-year, with average transaction size up +0.18%.30 Spending patterns reflected a shift toward essentials: grocery spending rose +3% year-over-year and mass merchants gained +7%, while apparel contracted -2% and department store spending fell -8%.30 Average hourly wages at +4.7% year-over-year ($37.73/hr) outpaced the +2.4% headline CPI, indicating positive real wage gains in March, though rising gasoline and food prices are compressing discretionary budgets.81 The pipeline tracks 142 tourism and culture projects ($21.9B) and 64 commercial/mixed-use projects ($27.5B) with exposure to consumer discretionary spending trends.

global.analysis:
The U.S. Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50-3.75% for its second consecutive meeting on March 18, maintaining a 125-150 basis point gap above the Bank of Canada's 2.25% overnight rate.31 March FOMC minutes indicated willingness to consider rate increases if inflation persists above target.31 Nonfarm payrolls added +178,000 jobs in March with unemployment at 4.3%.31 The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index fell to 50.8, the second-lowest reading since 1952.31 Both the BoC and the Fed announce rate decisions on April 29, a synchronized policy window that will set cross-border rate differentials affecting capital flows and the CAD/USD exchange rate.431

U.S. tariff policy continued to evolve: Section 232 tariffs were restructured to 50% on aluminum, steel, and copper, directly affecting Canadian metal exporters.16 Canada announced a six-month pause on retaliatory tariffs for U.S.-origin manufacturing, food/beverage, health care, and national security goods on April 15.16 The CUSMA/USMCA 2026 joint review is scheduled for July.25 Canadian merchandise exports to the U.S. fell -10% year-over-year while non-U.S. exports rose +17%, consistent with trade diversion.9 The pipeline tracks 45 manufacturing projects ($67.3B) and 305 mining projects ($146.0B) with U.S. trade policy exposure.

China's Q1 2026 GDP grew 5.0% year-over-year, beating the 4.8% consensus and accelerating from 4.5% in Q4 2025.32 Industrial production rose 6.1% year-over-year, with high-tech manufacturing up 12.5% and equipment manufacturing up 8.9%.32 March imports surged +27.8% year-over-year, the strongest since November 2021, while exports grew +2.5% year-over-year, decelerating from the combined January-February pace of +21.8%.32 Factory-gate prices turned positive for the first time in more than three years on commodity price strength.32 EV exports surged +78%, battery exports +50%, and wind equipment exports +45%.32

Bilateral Canada-China trade totaled C$124.8B in 2025.34 Minister Sidhu attended a consumer expo to advance trade partnerships, and Finance Minister Champagne engaged on bilateral trade.34 The Trans Mountain Expansion (TMX) pipeline provides an alternative export corridor for Asian buyers, independent of Strait of Hormuz transit routes.22 The pipeline tracks 305 mining projects ($146.0B) and 39 oil and gas projects ($97.3B) with exposure to Chinese commodity demand. China's import surge supports demand for Canadian iron ore, copper, potash, and energy products.

global.analysis:
The European Central Bank main refinancing rate stood at 2.15% with the deposit facility at 2.0%.33 Markets priced a hold at the April 29-30 meeting, with a hike to 2.5% or above expected in June.33 The ECB raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 2.6%, citing higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict.33 Eurozone HICP ran at +1.9% year-over-year in the latest available print.33

The BoC, Fed, and ECB all decide rates within the April 29-30 window — a synchronized global monetary policy moment. If the ECB hikes to 2.5% or above in June while the BoC holds at 2.25%, the narrowing rate differential could influence capital flows and the EUR/CAD cross rate. Global central banks are shifting from easing cycles to inflation response, with Hormuz-driven energy costs pushing headline inflation higher across advanced economies.334

The Bank of England base rate stood at 3.75%, 150 basis points above the Bank of Canada overnight rate.31 The next BoE decision is April 30. Brent crude — the dominant North Sea benchmark — stood at $95.42/bbl after rebounding from $90.38 on April 17 following Strait of Hormuz re-closure reports.22 The EIA modeled scenarios ranging from $110/bbl (one-quarter outage) to $132/bbl (two-quarter outage).35 The 150 basis point rate gap between the BoE and the BoC mirrors the Fed-BoC differential, reinforcing CAD cross-rate pressures across the pipeline's 39 oil and gas projects ($97.3B) and 550 power and energy projects ($490.9B) with sterling and Brent exposure.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's labour market held steady in March with unemployment unchanged at 7.6%, while the employment rate registered 59.7% and the participation rate 64.6%.1 The province's GDP grew at +1.2% in Q4 2025, tracking below the national average.2 Housing starts recorded 67,274 annualized units as of March 2026.3

The Ontario Budget 2026, tabled March 26, projects a $13.8B deficit for 2026-27 and commits $210B over ten years in capital spending, including $37B for the immediate fiscal year.1 The plan allocates $64B over a decade for health infrastructure encompassing 50 hospital projects and 3,000 new beds, plus $31B for highways with a Ring of Fire road targeted for June 2026.1

Bill 98 introduces development charge reductions of 30-50% for priority municipalities, intended to reduce costs for residential construction.4 A federal-Ontario housing partnership announced March 30 targets $2.2B in tax relief and an estimated 8,000 additional housing starts.5 The pipeline tracks 497 projects totalling $136.8B across the province, with 227 under construction.2 The Kinross Gold Great Bear Project in Red Lake ($5B+) entered the pipeline as a new discovery this period.2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy dominates Ontario's project pipeline by value, anchored by the $26B Adaptive Phased Management Deep Geological Repository (Proposed), the $13B Bruce Nuclear Refurbishment (Under Construction), and the $12.8B Darlington Refurbishment (Under Construction).1 Infrastructure accounts for 195 projects including the $12.6B Eglinton Crosstown LRT and $4.8B GO Transit Expansion.2 Healthcare leads by project count with 134 tracked projects aligned with the budget's 50-hospital commitment.1
provinces.labourDeepDive: Ontario's unemployment held at 7.6% in March, above the national rate of 6.7%.1 The employment rate of 59.7% and participation rate of 64.6% both trail the national averages of 60.6% and 64.9% respectively.3 The province's $210B capital plan targets construction employment across hospital, transit, and highway projects over the next decade.1
provinces.consumerPulse: Ontario CPI registered a month-over-month decline of 1.8 points in March 2026, reflecting easing price pressures in the province.2 The federal fuel excise suspension effective April 14 through September 7 applies nationally but disproportionately affects Ontario given the province's 5.9 million registered vehicles.5 The $2.2B federal-Ontario housing partnership targets affordability through tax relief measures.5
provinces.marketContext: WTI crude at $86.25/bbl has limited direct impact on Ontario's economy relative to western provinces, though the province's 15 tracked power and energy projects ($51.8B combined) include refinery and pipeline-linked assets sensitive to commodity price volatility.
provinces.tradeExposure: Ontario's manufacturing sector accounts for approximately 45% of Canadian auto production; the US absorbs over 75% of Ontario goods exports, with auto parts, vehicles, and machinery as leading categories.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec's unemployment rate fell to 5.4% in March, a 0.5 percentage point month-over-month decline that places the province well below the national 6.7% rate.1 The employment rate stood at 60.7% with participation at 64.5%.1 GDP growth registered +1.3% in Q4 2025.2

Quebec Budget 2026-27 commits $1.7B over five years for economic transformation and a $167B infrastructure plan covering hospitals, transit, and housing.2 The federal government announced $63.9M for 99 Quebec steel-sector SMEs as part of tariff response measures.3 A Canada-Quebec housing partnership delivered 865 new affordable homes through a $200M investment.4

The pipeline tracks 429 projects totalling $75.9B, with education (118 projects) and infrastructure (100 projects) as the most active sectors by count.2 Housing starts reached 53,461 annualized units.5 The Parc eolien zone Chamouchouane ($9B, Proposed) leads the value pipeline, followed by the Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.9B, Under Construction) and Quebec City Tramway ($3.8B, Under Construction).2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy projects lead Quebec by value with 29 tracked projects, anchored by the $9B Chamouchouane wind farm (Proposed), $4B green hydrogen facility (Under Review), and $2.2B Champlain Hudson Power Express transmission line (Under Construction).2 Infrastructure follows with 100 projects including the Blue Line Extension and TramCite. Education accounts for 118 projects, the highest sector count in Quebec's pipeline.2
provinces.labourDeepDive: Quebec recorded the sharpest unemployment improvement among provinces in March, dropping 0.5 percentage points to 5.4%.1 The employment rate of 60.7% slightly exceeds the national 60.6%. The province's $63.9M federal steel-sector investment targets retention of 99 SME employers across the province.3 Construction employment remains supported by 36 projects under construction and 279 approved projects in the pipeline.2
provinces.consumerPulse: Quebec CPI rose 0.6 points month-over-month in March 2026, the lowest provincial increase among major provinces.1 The Canada-Quebec housing partnership targets affordability with 865 new units and $200M in combined investment.4 Quebec's 53,461 annualized housing starts represent the second-highest provincial total after Ontario.5
provinces.marketContext: Quebec's hydroelectric exports and aluminum production link the province to electricity pricing and base metals markets. The $2.2B Champlain Hudson Power Express enables direct power exports to New York, providing revenue diversification beyond domestic demand.
provinces.tradeExposure: Quebec exports approximately $90B annually, with aerospace, aluminum, forestry products, and electricity as primary categories. The United States receives roughly 70% of Quebec goods exports.

provinces.analysis:
Alberta recorded unemployment at 6.3% in March 2026 with the highest employment rate among provinces at 64.4% and participation at 68.7%.1 GDP grew +2.7% in Q4 2025, leading major provinces.2 CPI rose 4.8 points month-over-month, the highest provincial increase, reflecting energy-price pass-through.1

Alberta Budget 2026 projects a $9.4B deficit driven by non-renewable resource revenues declining $8.8B from 2024-25 levels.3 WTI crude volatility — ranging from US$128/bbl (April 2 peak) to US$83.85/bbl (April 17) before recovering to ~$86.25/bbl — directly affects provincial royalty revenue forecasts.4

The pipeline tracks 657 projects totalling $291.9B, the highest provincial value. The province signed an IAAC cooperation agreement and a carbon pricing MOU with Ottawa at $130/tonne, while TIER fund credits remain frozen at $95/tonne.5 Data centre proposals have requested over 20 GW of power capacity, with the province targeting $100B in data centre investment.3
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy accounts for 125 projects led by the $16.5B Pathways Alliance Carbon Capture Hub (Proposed), $12B AOSP Jackpine (Approved), and $11.5B Dow Net-Zero Polyethylene Facility (Under Construction).2 Government projects total 143, the highest sector count. The $12B Wonder Valley AI Data Centre Park represents the emerging data infrastructure sector.2 Telus Infrastructure Upgrades ($19B) leads the overall pipeline by value.2
provinces.labourDeepDive: Alberta's 64.4% employment rate and 68.7% participation rate are the highest among provinces, reflecting strong labour demand in energy and construction.1 The 6.3% unemployment rate tracks below the national 6.7%. With 167 projects under construction and 349 proposed, the province's labour absorption capacity faces sustained demand across energy, data centre, and infrastructure sectors.2
provinces.consumerPulse: Alberta's CPI increased 4.8 points month-over-month in March, the highest among provinces, driven by gasoline price spikes during the Strait of Hormuz disruption.1 The federal fuel excise suspension (April 14 through September 7) provides partial relief. Housing starts totalled 48,438 annualized units.3 The $9.4B provincial deficit constrains fiscal capacity for consumer-facing programs.4
provinces.marketContext: Alberta's economy is directly linked to WTI crude ($86.25/bbl, down 32.7% from April 2 peak). The pipeline tracks 125 power/energy projects and the province's resource royalties declined $8.8B from 2024-25. The $130/tonne carbon price MOU affects 349 proposed projects in the oil sands and heavy industry sectors.
provinces.tradeExposure: Alberta exports approximately $130B annually, dominated by crude oil and natural gas (75%+ of exports). The United States receives over 90% of Alberta energy exports via pipelines including Trans Mountain and Keystone.

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.analysis:
British Columbia's unemployment rose to 6.7% in March, a 0.6 percentage point increase month-over-month described as the highest since February 2016.1 The employment rate registered 60.5% with participation at 64.4%.2 GDP grew +1.2% in Q4 2025.2

Mining permits reform took effect April 1 establishing new 40-140 day processing timelines as part of the province's effort to accelerate major project approvals.1 The 2025 exploration year was BC's strongest on record with spending up 36% year-over-year.3

The pipeline tracks 528 projects totalling $490.5B, with LNG Canada dominating — Phase 1 ($47.9B, Under Construction), the completed Facility ($40B), and proposed Phase 2 ($25B).4 Ksi Lisims LNG represents an additional $30B expected investment. Housing starts reached 41,331 annualized units.5 Short-term rental opt-out process was accelerated April 17 to provide communities flexibility for peak travel season.6
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy leads with 70 projects including LNG Canada Phase 1 ($47.9B), the $22B Kitimat Clean Oil Refinery (Under Review), and the $16B Peace River Site C (Under Construction).4 Mining accounts for 57 projects benefiting from the new permit processing timelines. Residential (51 projects) and transport/logistics (34) reflect housing and port infrastructure demand.2
provinces.labourDeepDive: BC's +0.6pp unemployment increase to 6.7% was the sharpest deterioration among provinces in March.1 The employment rate of 60.5% trails the national 60.6%. With 146 projects under construction and 149 proposed, the construction sector maintains demand, though 29 projects remain on hold and 26 have been cancelled.2
provinces.consumerPulse: BC CPI rose 1.3 points month-over-month in March, moderate relative to Alberta's 4.8.2 Housing starts at 41,331 annualized units face headwinds from the rising unemployment rate. The accelerated short-term rental opt-out process (April 17) addresses vacancy rates in communities with healthy rental markets.6
provinces.marketContext: BC's resource economy links to LNG pricing (Henry Hub, JKM Asia), copper, and forestry products. The LNG Canada Phase 1 completion timeline positions BC as a Pacific-facing energy exporter. Gold and copper exploration spending rose 36% YoY in 2025, reflecting commodity price incentives.
provinces.tradeExposure: BC exports approximately $50B annually through Pacific gateways, with forestry products, coal, LNG (emerging), and minerals as leading categories. Asia-Pacific markets (China, Japan, South Korea) receive approximately 50% of BC exports.

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan recorded the lowest provincial unemployment rate at 5.0% in March, a 0.6 percentage point decline month-over-month.1 The employment rate of 63.4% and participation rate of 67.1% both rank among the highest nationally.2 GDP grew +3.4% in Q4 2025, the strongest among provinces.2

The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission approved two uranium mines — Denison Mines' Wheeler River ($420M) and NexGen Energy's Rook 1 ($1.5B) — the first uranium mine approvals in Canada since 2004.1 Combined, these projects represent $2.8B in investment, 1,600+ construction jobs, and 700+ operational jobs.1

The pipeline tracks 123 projects totalling $28.4B. BHP's Jansen Stage 1 ($7.5B) and Stage 2 ($6.4B) potash mines are both under construction, positioning Saskatchewan to expand global potash market share.3 Housing starts totalled 5,486 annualized units.2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Mining dominates Saskatchewan's high-value pipeline with 11 tracked projects led by Jansen Stage 1 ($7.5B), Jansen Stage 2 ($6.4B), Rook I ($1.3B, Approved), and Wheeler River ($420M).1 Power and energy accounts for 12 projects including the $2B FCL HDRD Plant (Proposed) and $1.3B Aspen Power Station (Under Construction). Infrastructure counts 16 projects.3
provinces.labourDeepDive: Saskatchewan's 5.0% unemployment is 1.7 percentage points below the national rate. The 0.6pp monthly decline was the largest improvement among provinces.1 The two new uranium mine approvals add an estimated 1,600+ construction jobs and 700+ permanent operational positions, with construction timelines extending through 2028-2030.1
provinces.consumerPulse: Saskatchewan CPI increased 1.0 point month-over-month, moderate relative to the Alberta-driven energy price spike.2 The province's strong labour market (lowest unemployment, high participation) supports consumer spending. Housing starts at 5,486 reflect the province's smaller population base.2
provinces.marketContext: Saskatchewan's economy links to potash (global fertilizer markets), uranium (spot $80+/lb), wheat, and oil. BHP's $13.9B combined Jansen investment positions the province as the world's largest potash producer. The two new uranium mine approvals coincide with uranium prices near decade highs.
provinces.tradeExposure: Saskatchewan exports approximately $40B annually, dominated by potash, uranium, wheat, canola, and crude oil. The United States, China, India, and Japan are primary trading partners for agricultural and mineral exports.

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.analysis:
Manitoba's unemployment held at 5.6% in March, below the national 6.7% rate.1 The employment rate stood at 62.5% with participation at 66.3%.1 GDP grew +1.1% in Q4 2025.2 Housing starts reached 7,642 annualized units.2

Manitoba Budget 2026 includes a record $3.8B capital investment.3 The Port of Churchill is receiving $262.5M in federal-provincial funding over five years.3 A Canada-Manitoba 'one project, one review' cooperation agreement was signed April 14, streamlining environmental assessments for major projects.4

The pipeline tracks 2,023 projects totalling $6.5B, with 1,976 under review. Winnipeg's draft 2026 budget includes capital spending up 75%.5 Key infrastructure projects include the $502M North End Sewage Treatment Plant upgrades (Approved), $495M Lake Manitoba/Lake St. Martin Outlet Channels (Approved), and the $387M Pointe du Bois Renewable Energy Project (Under Construction).3
provinces.sectorHighlights: Infrastructure leads Manitoba's pipeline with projects totalling over $1.7B including the $502M NEWPCC Biosolids Facilities, $495M Lake Manitoba/St. Martin outlet channels, $386M Manitoba Floodway Expansion, and $300M Winnipeg Street Renewal.3 Water and wastewater accounts for 455 projects under review. The $387M Pointe du Bois Renewable Energy Project anchors the power/energy sector.3
provinces.labourDeepDive: Manitoba's 5.6% unemployment rate held steady in March, 1.1pp below the national average.1 The employment rate of 62.5% and participation rate of 66.3% both exceed national figures. The record $3.8B capital budget and 75% increase in Winnipeg capital spending signal construction employment growth ahead.3
provinces.consumerPulse: Manitoba CPI rose 3.4 points month-over-month in March, above the national average, reflecting transportation fuel costs.1 The federal fuel excise suspension (April 14 to September 7) provides temporary relief. Housing starts at 7,642 annualized units reflect moderate residential construction activity.2
provinces.marketContext: Manitoba's economy links to agricultural commodities (wheat, canola), hydroelectric exports, and nickel mining. The Port of Churchill ($262.5M investment) positions the province as an Arctic shipping gateway for grain exports to European and Asian markets.
provinces.tradeExposure: Manitoba exports approximately $18B annually, with agricultural products, manufactured goods, and electricity as leading categories. The United States receives approximately 65% of Manitoba exports; the Port of Churchill enables grain shipments to Europe and Asia.

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia's unemployment fell to 6.6% in March, a 0.5 percentage point month-over-month decline.1 The employment rate of 57.0% and participation rate of 61.3% remain below national averages, reflecting the province's older demographic profile.1 GDP grew +2.7% in Q4 2025, tied with Alberta for the strongest growth rate.2

The Powering the Economy Act passed April 9, enabling offshore wind and subsurface energy development.3 Budget 2026-27 includes a $3.5B+ capital plan.4 The federal Housing Infrastructure Fund allocates $170.9M over 10 years for water and wastewater infrastructure.5

The pipeline tracks 295 projects totalling $13B, with 233 complete. The $8B Bear Head Energy project (Proposed) leads by value, followed by the $367M Boat Harbour Remediation (Approved) and $354M NSP Battery Storage (Approved).4 Housing starts reached 7,146 annualized units.2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Clean energy leads Nova Scotia's emerging pipeline with 71 projects, supported by the Powering the Economy Act enabling offshore wind development.3 The $8B Bear Head Energy project (hydrogen/ammonia, Proposed) would be the largest single investment in provincial history. NSP Battery Storage ($354M, Approved) addresses grid reliability. Infrastructure accounts for 43 combined projects.4
provinces.labourDeepDive: Nova Scotia's 0.5pp unemployment decline to 6.6% parallels Quebec's improvement.1 The 57.0% employment rate reflects an older population with lower workforce participation. Immigration-driven population growth continues to expand the labour supply. The $3.5B+ capital plan and offshore energy legislation signal future construction demand.4
provinces.consumerPulse: Nova Scotia CPI rose 1.7 points month-over-month, moderate within the Atlantic region.1 Housing starts at 7,146 annualized units reflect ongoing demand driven by population growth through immigration. The $170.9M Housing Infrastructure Fund addresses water/wastewater constraints that limit new residential development.5
provinces.marketContext: Nova Scotia's emerging energy economy links to offshore wind, hydrogen (Bear Head $8B), and battery storage. The Powering the Economy Act positions the province for participation in the Atlantic offshore wind supply chain. Lobster and seafood exports remain the primary commodity link.
provinces.tradeExposure: Nova Scotia exports approximately $7B annually, led by seafood (lobster), tires, forestry products, and emerging energy products. The United States and European Union are primary trading partners.

provinces.name: New Brunswick
provinces.analysis:
New Brunswick's unemployment held at 7.0% in March, above the national 6.7%.1 The employment rate registered 56.5% with participation at 60.7%, both below national figures reflecting the province's older demographic.1 GDP grew +1.8% in Q4 2025.2

Premier Susan Holt met Prime Minister Carney on April 20-21 to advance defence investment, energy infrastructure, and critical minerals priorities.3 Irving Oil Refinery is expanding hydrogen capacity, becoming the first Canadian refinery to purchase a hydrogen electrolyzer.3 NB Power released its 2026 Integrated Resource Plan targeting 1,400 MW of new wind capacity by 2035.4

The pipeline tracks 166 projects totalling $4.9B, with 46 under construction. The Sisson Brook tungsten mine was selected for federal fast-track permitting.3 The $1.1B Saint John Pulp Mill Upgrades (Under Review) leads by value, followed by the $579M Sisson Project (Approved) and $420M Trans-Canada Highway twinning (Under Construction).2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Energy infrastructure dominates New Brunswick's current development trajectory. Irving Oil's hydrogen electrolyzer investment represents a refinery modernization shift.3 NB Power's 1,400 MW wind target by 2035 signals substantial renewable procurement.4 The $147M Smart Grid Investments (Under Construction) supports grid modernization. Forestry/pulp anchors manufacturing with the $1.1B Saint John mill upgrade.2
provinces.labourDeepDive: New Brunswick's 7.0% unemployment and 56.5% employment rate reflect structural demographic challenges — the province has one of Canada's oldest populations.1 The 46 projects under construction and federal fast-track designation for the Sisson tungsten mine provide near-term construction employment. The 1,400 MW wind buildout would sustain multi-year construction demand.4
provinces.consumerPulse: New Brunswick CPI rose 2.4 points month-over-month in March, matching the national CPI level.1 Housing starts at 6,011 annualized units reflect modest residential construction. The province's reliance on Irving Oil refinery output connects local gasoline pricing to the Strait of Hormuz disruption and WTI volatility.2
provinces.marketContext: New Brunswick's energy economy centres on Irving Oil (Canada's largest refinery), NB Power nuclear and hydro generation, and emerging wind capacity. The refinery's hydrogen expansion links to the global hydrogen economy. Defence procurement connects to 5 Wing Gagetown and naval shipbuilding supply chains.
provinces.tradeExposure: New Brunswick exports approximately $15B annually, led by refined petroleum products (Irving Oil), seafood, forestry products, and potash. The United States receives approximately 85% of exports; the Irving refinery also ships to European markets.

provinces.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's unemployment rose to 9.5% in March, a 0.3 percentage point increase and the highest provincial rate.1 The employment rate of 52.7% and participation rate of 58.1% are the lowest nationally.1 GDP grew +2.4% in Q4 2025, supported by offshore oil production gains.2

The Bay du Nord agreement was signed March 3 with Equinor and BP — an estimated $14B investment representing the first new standalone offshore development since Hebron, with first oil expected 2031.3 February 2026 offshore production reached 8.7 million barrels, up 69.2% year-over-year, with production value of $837.2M (up 51.7% YoY).4

The pipeline tracks 1,510 projects totalling $23.9B. Federal defence investments were announced at 5 Wing Goose Bay.5 The $10B Grassy Point LNG (Proposed) and $3.9B Kamistiatusset iron ore mine (Under Review) round out the high-value pipeline.2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Offshore oil and gas dominates Newfoundland's economy, with February production of 8.7M barrels (+69.2% YoY) valued at $837.2M.4 Power/energy projects include the $10B Grassy Point LNG and White Rose Expansion ($3.8B + $2.3B, both Under Construction).2 Mining contributes the $3.9B Kamistiatusset (Kami) iron ore project and $534M Valentine Gold Mine (Under Construction).2
provinces.labourDeepDive: Newfoundland's 9.5% unemployment rate is the highest among provinces, 2.8pp above the national average.1 The 52.7% employment rate reflects seasonal fisheries patterns, aging demographics, and out-migration. The Bay du Nord project ($14B) is projected to generate significant construction employment through the late 2020s, with first oil in 2031.3
provinces.consumerPulse: Newfoundland CPI rose 2.3 points month-over-month in March.1 The province's dependence on imported goods via ferry and air results in structurally higher consumer prices. Housing starts at 1,223 annualized units reflect limited residential demand given population decline. Offshore production value of $837.2M in February supports provincial fiscal capacity.4
provinces.marketContext: Newfoundland's economy is directly tied to offshore oil production (Brent crude $95.42/bbl). February production of 8.7M barrels (+69.2% YoY) demonstrates the impact of higher prices and Hibernia/Terra Nova operations. The Bay du Nord $14B commitment signals long-term offshore viability despite energy transition pressures.
provinces.tradeExposure: Newfoundland and Labrador exports approximately $12B annually, dominated by crude oil (offshore production), iron ore (Labrador), and seafood. European and US East Coast markets receive the majority of offshore crude shipments.

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island's unemployment edged up 0.1 percentage points to 7.3% in March.1 The employment rate of 61.8% and participation rate of 66.6% both exceed national averages.1 GDP grew +3.6% in Q4 2025, the second-highest among provinces after Saskatchewan.2

PEI Budget 2026-27 was tabled April 14 with a deficit of $409.9M (3.5% of GDP).3 Debt-to-GDP is rising to 38.1%, projected to reach approximately 40% — the highest since at least 1986-87.4 Federal Build Communities Strong Fund investment was announced for water and wastewater infrastructure in Cornwall.5

The pipeline tracks 78 projects totalling $1.5B, with 70 under construction. Infrastructure (39 projects) and power/energy (13 projects) lead by count. The $92M Northumberland Strait Submarine Transmission System (Under Construction) and $85M Skinners Pond Wind Energy Centre (Proposed) anchor the energy pipeline.2
provinces.sectorHighlights: Infrastructure accounts for 39 of PEI's 78 tracked projects, dominated by road resurfacing and bridge programs.2 Power and energy (13 projects) includes the $92M Northumberland Strait submarine cable, $85M Skinners Pond wind farm, and $80M PEIEC Wind Farm #5 (Under Construction).2 Tourism and culture (16 projects) reflects the province's seasonal economy diversification efforts.2
provinces.labourDeepDive: PEI's 7.3% unemployment rate is 0.6pp above the national average despite strong GDP growth.1 The 66.6% participation rate exceeds the national 64.9%, indicating broad workforce engagement. The province's small labour market (~90,000 employed) means individual project starts have outsized employment effects.1
provinces.consumerPulse: PEI recorded the highest provincial CPI increase at 7.3 points month-over-month in March, reflecting the province's exposure to imported goods and fuel costs.1 The $409.9M deficit and rising debt-to-GDP ratio (38.1%, approaching 40%) constrain fiscal capacity for consumer relief measures.3 Housing starts at 963 annualized units reflect limited construction capacity.2
provinces.marketContext: PEI's economy links to agricultural commodities (potatoes, seafood), tourism, and wind energy. The Northumberland Strait submarine transmission cable connects the province to mainland electricity markets. The island's small scale means individual project decisions have proportionally large economic effects.
provinces.tradeExposure: PEI exports approximately $2B annually, led by potatoes, seafood (lobster, mussels), and aerospace components. The United States receives the majority of agricultural exports; the province's island geography necessitates marine and air transport for all trade.

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Yukon recorded unemployment at 3.9% in February 2026, the lowest rate among all provinces and territories.1 GDP contracted 3.3% in 2024, reflecting the cyclical nature of the territory's mining-dependent economy.2

The Yukon and federal governments approved BMC Minerals' Kudz Ze Kayah copper/lead/zinc mine on April 15 — the project will process up to 2 million tonnes of ore annually over 10 years and is expected to become Canada's largest zinc producer.1 The approval carries 52 terms and conditions. Ross River Dena Council stated the approval was issued without informed consent.1

The pipeline tracks 97 projects totalling $46.3B, dominated by the $40B Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment (Proposed). Mining projects include the $3.6B Casino Mine (Proposed), $489M Kudz Ze Kayah (Under Review), and $317M Coffee Gold Mine (Under Review).2 Mineral exploration spending reached $313M in 2025.3
provinces.sectorHighlights: Mining anchors Yukon's private-sector economy with the Casino Mine ($3.6B), Kudz Ze Kayah ($489M, newly approved), and Coffee Gold ($317M).1 Mineral exploration spending of $313M in 2025 reflects sustained interest.3 Defence represents the largest single commitment at $40B (Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment, Proposed). Infrastructure accounts for 55 projects including the $363M Yukon Resource Gateway Project (Under Construction).2
provinces.labourDeepDive: Yukon's 3.9% unemployment is the lowest in Canada, reflecting a tight labour market in the territory's small workforce (~24,000 employed).1 The Kudz Ze Kayah mine approval signals multi-year construction employment ahead. The $363M Resource Gateway Project (road infrastructure) is currently under construction providing direct employment.2
provinces.consumerPulse: Yukon's northern location results in structurally higher consumer costs due to transportation premiums on imported goods. The federal fuel excise suspension (April 14 through September 7) provides proportionally greater relief given longer driving distances and higher per-capita fuel consumption. The territory's low unemployment supports household spending capacity.1
provinces.marketContext: Yukon's economy links to zinc, copper, gold, and lead prices. The Kudz Ze Kayah mine (Canada's expected largest zinc producer) ties the territory directly to LME zinc pricing. Gold exploration (Casino, Coffee) connects to the $2,300+/oz gold market. Defence spending provides a non-commodity anchor.
provinces.tradeExposure: Yukon's mineral exports flow primarily to Asian smelters and US markets. The territory's small economy means individual mine openings or closures have outsized GDP effects. The Resource Gateway road project improves access to tidewater for mineral shipments.

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
Northwest Territories recorded unemployment at 5.3% in February 2026.1 GDP contracted 1.1% in 2024 as diamond mining operations wound down.2

The Diavik Mine (Rio Tinto) is closing in March 2026 after exhausting ore reserves. The territory's three diamond mines employed 1,500+ residents and contributed approximately 20% of NWT GDP.2 The territory is targeting critical minerals as an economic replacement — NWT contains nearly three-quarters of minerals on Canada's critical minerals list.2

The pipeline tracks 175 projects totalling $40.2B, dominated by the $35B Arctic Defence and Infrastructure Spending Package (Proposed).1 Mining projects in the pipeline include Pine Point ($653M, Under Review), NICO Cobalt-Gold-Bismuth ($589M, Approved), and Prairie Creek ($474M, Approved).1 The $1.2B Taltson Hydroelectricity Expansion (Under Construction) addresses power supply constraints for future mining operations.1
provinces.sectorHighlights: Mining faces structural transition as Diavik closes. Critical minerals replacement projects include Pine Point zinc/lead ($653M), NICO cobalt/gold/bismuth ($589M), and Prairie Creek zinc/lead ($474M).2 The $1.2B Taltson Hydroelectricity Expansion provides power infrastructure for future mining. Defence represents the largest value commitment at $35B for Arctic sovereignty infrastructure.1
provinces.labourDeepDive: NWT's 5.3% unemployment rate masks structural challenges from the Diavik closure. The 1,500+ mining jobs (direct) represent a substantial portion of the territory's approximately 23,000-person workforce.2 Tlicho Government, YKDFN, and GNWT have partnered to support affected residents and transition to critical minerals employment.1
provinces.consumerPulse: NWT faces the highest consumer costs in Canada due to Arctic transportation premiums and limited local production. The Diavik closure reduces territorial income and tax base, with implications for government service capacity. The federal fuel excise suspension provides partial relief for a population heavily dependent on long-distance road and air transport for essential goods.2
provinces.marketContext: NWT's economy is transitioning from diamonds (Diavik closing) to critical minerals. The territory's mineral endowment covers nearly three-quarters of Canada's critical minerals list. Arctic defence spending ($35B proposed) provides a non-resource anchor. The Taltson expansion addresses the power constraint that has historically limited mining development.
provinces.tradeExposure: NWT diamond exports historically dominated the territory's trade profile, flowing to Antwerp and Mumbai cutting centres. Critical minerals (cobalt, bismuth, zinc) target emerging battery and technology supply chains. Arctic shipping routes (emerging) may provide future trade advantages.

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut recorded unemployment at 10.8% in February 2026, the highest rate among all provinces and territories.1 GDP grew +7.5% in 2024, the strongest growth nationally, driven by mining expansion.2

The Nunavut Mining Symposium (April 20-22) in Iqaluit is covering updates from Baffinland, Agnico Eagle, and B2Gold.1 The Grays Bay Road and Port project is advancing to environmental assessment — it would be Canada's first deep-water Arctic Ocean port and could increase Nunavut GDP by 18%.3

The pipeline tracks 37 projects totalling $1.9B, with 30 under construction. The $610M Back River Gold Project (B2Gold, Under Construction) leads by value, followed by the $214M Iqaluit Water Infrastructure Improvement Project and $125M Powerplant Upgrades across four communities.2 Baffinland Mary River Steensby Component consultation concluded, with rail-and-port construction planned for 2026.3
provinces.sectorHighlights: Mining drives Nunavut's private-sector economy, anchored by the $610M Back River Gold Project (Under Construction) and Baffinland's Mary River iron ore operations.2 Infrastructure accounts for 13 projects addressing the territory's severe infrastructure deficit, including the $214M Iqaluit water project and $85M marine infrastructure.2 The Grays Bay Road and Port would create Canada's first deep-water Arctic port, enabling year-round mineral exports.3
provinces.labourDeepDive: Nunavut's 10.8% unemployment rate reflects structural challenges: limited economic diversity, small population dispersed across remote communities, and seasonal employment patterns.1 Mining operations (Back River, Mary River) provide the primary source of private-sector wage employment. The Grays Bay Road and Port project could generate multi-year construction employment.3
provinces.consumerPulse: Nunavut has the highest cost of living among Canadian jurisdictions, with food prices in remote communities averaging 2-3 times southern Canadian levels due to air freight dependence. The $125M powerplant upgrade program addresses energy costs in Cambridge Bay, Gjoa Haven, Igloolik, and Iqaluit. The $214M Iqaluit water infrastructure project addresses essential services.2
provinces.marketContext: Nunavut's economy links to gold ($2,300+/oz), iron ore (Mary River), and federal transfer payments. The Grays Bay Road and Port project would connect mineral deposits to global markets via Arctic shipping. The territory's GDP growth of +7.5% (2024) reflects mine production ramp-up and construction activity.
provinces.tradeExposure: Nunavut exports primarily iron ore (Baffinland Mary River to European steel markets) and gold (Back River to global markets). The proposed Grays Bay port would enable copper, zinc, and other mineral exports from the Slave Geological Province to Asian markets via the Northwest Passage.

goods_industries.name: Manufacturing
goods_industries.employment_trend: EV battery plants adding jobs; traditional auto declining
goods_industries.analysis: Aluminum at $3,423/lb, copper at $5.53/lb, and nickel (linked to EV battery supply chains) form the key input costs for Canadian manufacturing.1 Auto production is expected to decline approximately 4% in 2026, following 2025 output of 1.2M+ vehicles (-5.4% YoY).2 Auto exports fell 21.2% to $5.4B in January 2026 (the lowest since September 2021), then recovered 30.2% in February.2 The federal government allocated $3B through the Strategic Response Fund plus $100M via the Regional Tariff Response Initiative for the auto sector.3 EV sales targets stand at 75% by 2035 and 90% by 2040.3 VW PowerCo's St. Thomas gigafactory completed primary concrete foundations and will become Canada's largest manufacturing plant.4 NextStar Energy in Windsor commenced battery module production.4 An additional $11.7M was allocated for 15 EV charging projects installing 1,600+ chargers nationally.5 The pipeline tracks 49 projects valued at $67.3B, including the Dow Fort Saskatchewan Path2Zero expansion ($10.1B).5

services_industries.name: Wholesale Trade

services_industries.name: Retail Trade
services_industries.employment_trend: Mixed; grocery and mass merchants hiring, department stores contracting

services_industries.name: Transportation & Warehousing

services_industries.name: Information & Cultural Industries
services_industries.employment_trend: Growing; AI and cloud infrastructure driving demand

services_industries.name: Finance & Insurance

services_industries.employment_trend: Mixed; industrial absorption recovering, office leasing stabilizing

financialMarkets.market_commentary:
Canadian and global markets navigated a week defined by Strait of Hormuz volatility and shifting rate expectations. The S&P/TSX Composite closed near 34,270 on April 18, advancing +2.3% over the period as financials offset energy sector weakness.1 Banks led gains — BMO rose +1.65% and Bank of Nova Scotia added +2.03% — as investors repositioned toward rate-sensitive sectors following bond market repricing of the Bank of Canada path.2 Energy names moved in the opposite direction: Canadian Natural Resources declined -7.28% and Suncor fell -4% as WTI collapsed from its April 2 peak near $128/bbl to $83.85 on April 17 before rebounding to $86.25 on re-closure reports.3

The Canadian dollar strengthened to 0.7305 USD (+1.5% over the period), supported by crude's partial recovery and narrowing Canada-U.S. rate differentials.4 Gold traded near $4,828/oz, up +9.09% over the past month and +40.03% year-over-year, as geopolitical uncertainty sustained safe-haven demand.5

Bond markets priced ~41 basis points of tightening by year-end, a material shift from rate-cut expectations that prevailed through Q1. The 2-year Government of Canada yield rose 35 basis points, producing a bear-flattening dynamic ahead of the April 29 BoC decision.6 This repricing affects financing assumptions for 4,471 active projects (Proposed, Under Review, and Approved status) representing the bulk of the $1,161.7B tracked pipeline.7 The pipeline's 550 power and energy projects ($490.9B) and 39 oil and gas projects ($97.3B) carry direct exposure to Hormuz-driven commodity price swings, while 305 mining projects ($146.0B) benefit from gold's advance toward record levels.7

fx.fx_commentary: The Canadian dollar advanced to 0.7305 USD (USD/CAD ~1.369), gaining +1.5% over the period as WTI's rebound from its April 17 trough supported the commodity-linked currency.1 Forecasters project USD/CAD in the 1.37-1.40 range near-term, with potential strengthening toward 1.34 by year-end if BoC tightening materializes.2 The Canada-U.S. rate differential narrowed as bond markets priced ~41 basis points of BoC tightening by December, while the Fed is expected to hold at 3.50%-3.75%.3 The euro gained on ECB hawkish signaling, while the yen strengthened on safe-haven demand. yieldCurve.yield_commentary: The Government of Canada yield curve steepened at the front end while bear-flattening at longer tenors. The 2-year yield rose 35 basis points as markets repriced BoC rate expectations from cuts to potential tightening.5 The 5-year benchmark — the reference rate for most fixed-rate mortgages and project financing — stood at 3.06%, down 0.13 percentage points over the past month but up 0.26 percentage points year-over-year.5 The 10-year traded at approximately 3.48%. Bond market pricing implies a ~92% probability of hold at the April 29 decision, with tightening expected later in 2026.6 The 10-year/2-year spread of 56 basis points reflects market expectations for higher near-term policy rates relative to long-run neutral, signaling a normalization cycle rather than recessionary inversion.5

commodity_commentary:
Commodity markets this week remained dominated by Strait of Hormuz developments and their cascading effects across the energy complex. WTI crude's 34% collapse from its April 2 peak of approximately $128/bbl to the April 17 trough of $83.85 represented the most violent price swing since March 2020, before re-closure reports drove a rebound to $86.25.1 The Brent-WTI spread widened as seaborne supply risk commanded a premium, with OPEC+ production declining 9.4 mb/d during the blockade period.2

Precious metals sustained gains with gold near $4,828/oz — up +40% year-over-year — reflecting geopolitical hedging and central bank reserve diversification.4 Base metals advanced on China's stronger-than-expected Q1 GDP of +5.0% and industrial production growth of +6.1%.5 Iron ore benefited from China's March imports surging +27.8% year-over-year.5

Construction-linked commodities presented a mixed picture: lumber remained soft as Canadian building permits fell -8.4% and housing starts missed consensus, while copper held firm on electrification demand despite U.S. 50% Section 232 tariffs on imports.67 The pipeline's 550 power and energy projects, 305 mining projects, and 39 oil and gas projects — collectively valued at $734.2B — carry direct commodity price exposure to these movements.3
